extracted.intended_audience: writers, literary critics, students and theorists of comedy/humour
extracted.subtask_description: A theoretical guide to the mechanisms that produce the comic in language and character, intended to help analyse or create humorous sentences, scenes and characters. Emphasises linguistic devices (inversion, pun, transposition) and character-based devices (rigidity, automatism, gesture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion (comic transformation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversing elements of a sentence (e.g., putting the subject in place of the object and vice versa) to obtain a new comic meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as the least interesting of the three fundamental laws but easy to apply; commonly used by professional wits to refute an idea humorously. Example: neighbour exchanges 'emptying your pipe on to my terrace' / 'putting your terrace under my pipe.' Many examples possible; simple inversion can produce comical refutation or reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference / play of two meanings in one sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Bracketing in the same expression two independent meanings that apparently tally so the sentence conveys two sets of ideas at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes a spectrum from pun (the least reputable form, where two different sentences merely sound the same) to true play upon words (one sentence genuinely expressing two ideas). True play upon words can approach poetic metaphor; it often relies on a word’s multiple meanings, especially figurative vs literal uses. The play upon words betrays a momentary lapse of attention in language and is amusing for that reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition (comic transformation of expression into another key)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposing the natural expression of an idea into another key or environment so that the same idea reads differently and becomes comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rule: 'A COMIC EFFECT IS ALWAYS OBTAINABLE BY TRANSPOSING THE NATURE EXPRESSION OF AN IDEA INTO ANOTHER KEY.' Transposition is far-reaching and can produce a wide variety of comic effects from buffoonery to refined irony; language transposition is analogous to the dramatic device of repetition in situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody (transposing the solemn into the familiar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rendering serious, solemn, or classical matter in familiar, commonplace, or modern terms to comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: describing dawn 'like a lobster being boiled.' Parody is a form of transposition often perceived as degradation of dignity; it produces immediate comic contrast between registers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degradation as comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Making something that was formerly dignified or noble appear mean or trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seen as one form of transposition; philosophers have defined the laughable as a species of degradation, but this is only one route to comedy among many. Degradation works by contrast between former dignity and present triviality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration (speaking small as large)
rubrics_metrics.description: Representing small things as though they were large (or vice versa) — prolonged/systematic exaggeration creates comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggeration, when systematic, is especially comic and gives rise to mock-heroic effects (e.g., braggadocio). It is a striking form of transposition and can be used methodically for comedic persona.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upward transposition of moral value (respectable language for disreputable matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing scandalous or low-class behaviour in terms of the utmost respectability or in reputable language to comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly characteristic in English literature (Dickens, Thackeray). The effect can be intense despite brevity — even a single word can imply an entire system of transposition and reveal a 'moral organisation of immorality.' Example: official saying 'Your peculations are too extensive for an official of your rank.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition between the real and the ideal — Irony vs Humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the contrast between what is (real) and what ought to be (ideal): irony states what ought to be and pretends it is so; humour describes what is and pretends it ought to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony is oratorical and emphasises the ideal (can become strong, high-pressure eloquence); humour is scientific, delights in concrete terms and technical detail, and is the counterpart of irony. Both are forms of satire but differ in tone and method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional jargon / technical vocabulary transposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposing everyday or sentimental ideas into professional, technical, or business phraseology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can yield rich laughable effects: e.g., applying commercial formulas to social invitations or treating marriage as a business affair. Such transpositions can reach 'special profundity' when they disclose a character fault rather than merely a stylistic inconsistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition (in situation and language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arranging events or expressions so a scene or idea is reproduced between characters or circumstances; repetition is a classic method of comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition can be literal or involve transposing the same idea into a different key; in language it parallels transposition — presenting a transposed expression and relying on the audience to supply the natural one spontaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as social correction / 'snubbing'
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of laughter is social: to reprove absentmindedness and lack of adaptability to society — a kind of social ragging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy often humiliates the target (though lightly) and thereby seeks to correct unsociability; this social role explains why comedy belongs partly to life and partly to art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsociability / rigidity of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Any individual who goes his own way without adapting to social surroundings (rigidity, withdrawal into oneself) is liable to become comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic springs from a person's failure to model himself on his environment; therefore rigidity, inflexibility and social non-adaptability are productive traits for a comic character (Alceste example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arousing audience emotion (comic requires intellectual distance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy appeals to the intelligence and is incompatible with emotion; to make a vice or situation comic, it must not arouse sympathy, pity, or fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the depiction awakens strong sympathy or pity, laughter is impossible. The comic poet must use techniques to lull sensibility or blunt audience sympathy (isolation of feeling, emphasis on gesture rather than action, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation of feeling within the character (parasitic emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Depict the character’s feeling as isolated, rigid and parasitic, preventing it from infecting the spectator and thus making it comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an emotion does not permeate the whole personality (it remains a stranger inside the soul), it fails to be contagious and becomes comic — may manifest as puppet-like movements or sudden forgetfulness (Harpagon example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on gesture rather than action
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct attention to gestures (attitudes, movements, language expressing a mental state automatically) rather than to purposeful action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gesture is automatic, explosive and isolates part of the person, preventing emotional engagement; action is intentional and invites sympathy. Comedy emphasises gesture because it rouses the audience at the brink of indifference and prevents taking things seriously (Tartuffe example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatism / absentmindedness as comic root
rubrics_metrics.description: The essentially laughable is what is done automatically — involuntary gestures, unconscious remarks, and systematic absentmindedness produce comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic absentmindedness (e.g., Don Quixote) is particularly comic. Contradictions where characters condemn behaviours they themselves do also reveal obliviousness and produce laughter. The comic element is the part of the person of which he is unaware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters as types / stock characters (generality over individuality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy aims at the general: comic characters are types or ready-made categories that others can fall into; resemblance to a type is itself comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because words and social life emphasize genera over individuality, depicting characters as types (crystallised traits) is the object of high-class comedy. Comedy’s focus on the general distinguishes it from other arts that emphasise the individual or the particular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play upon words betrays a lapse of attention in language
rubrics_metrics.description: When language momentarily 'forgets' its normal function and accommodates things to itself (e.g., punning or double-meaning), that lapse of attention is amusing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Play upon words often resembles negligence in language; its comedic effect is tied to the sense that language has momentarily become mechanical or forgetful of its proper role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pun vs true play upon words — qualitative distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Pun: appearance of two meanings due to identical sound (two different sentences). True play upon words: one sentence genuinely expresses two sets of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pun is described as the least reputable method; by imperceptible stages one moves from pun to richer, true play upon words which can approach metaphor and produce subtler comedic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques to prevent spectator sympathy (lulling or blunting sensibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic poet uses (often unconsciously) methods to either lull sensibility into dreamy indifference or to throw 'a wet blanket' over sympathy at the critical moment so a serious situation is not taken seriously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two broad methods: isolating feelings within the character (so they don't spread) and directing attention to gesture rather than action. Both reduce the spectator’s emotional engagement, enabling laughter.
